statement: In a 3 by 3 grid, the top-left and top-middle squares are shaded. How many more squares, at least, must be shaded so that both middle lines and both diagonals are mirror lines?

choices.misconception: I only made the picture match across the up-and-down middle line, so I shaded just the top-right square.
I gave the picture a half turn and shaded the two squares the shaded ones land on, but a half turn is not a mirror line.
I shaded all four corners but forgot that the top-middle square needs copies on the other three sides.
I made the picture symmetric across and down only, and forgot to check the two diagonal lines.

hints: Where does each shaded square go when reflected in each line?

Reflect each shaded square in all four mirror lines, and keep reflecting the new squares too, until nothing new appears. Corner squares only ever land on corners; middle-of-side squares land on middles of sides.
The top-left corner forces all four corners. The top-middle square forces all four middle-of-side squares. That is 8 squares in all, and 2 are already shaded.

solutions.reliable: Reflecting the top-left corner in the up-and-down line gives the top-right corner; reflecting those in the across line gives the bottom two corners. So all 4 corners must be shaded. Reflecting the top-middle square in the across line gives the bottom-middle; in a diagonal it goes to the left-middle or right-middle. So all 4 middle-of-side squares must be shaded. The picture is then every square except the centre, which is symmetric in all four lines. That is 8 shaded squares, 2 already done, so 6 extra. The transferable idea: a figure with several mirror lines must contain every image of every part.
solutions.elegant: The four lines of a square swap the four corners among themselves and the four side-middles among themselves. One shaded corner means all four; one shaded side-middle means all four: $4 + 4 - 2 = 6$ extra.

whyOnTest: Symmetry questions test applying every mirror line, not just the obvious one, and noticing which squares can swap places.
author: Devansh Sanghavi
